reasons: Scope 4: of the 157 terms, two large groups get no real space. comment: An accurate and well-ordered lesson: inner ear, then two ears, then the room, then comfort, then soundscape. It reads at the right level. fixes: SCOPE: after "A very short sound also seems quieter than a longer one at the same level." add: "What we heard just before also matters. A sound can seem softer after a long loud sound, or louder next to a quiet one. Researchers turn all of these effects into loudness models, which calculate loudness from a measured sound." (Cut words elsewhere to stay at or under 480.) FLOW: "Hearing damage can also change how loud sounds seem to each ear. A damaged ear may miss soft sounds, yet loud sounds seem almost normal. So loudness rises very fast as the volume increases." -> "Each ear does this work on its own, and a damaged ear does it differently. It may miss soft sounds, yet loud sounds seem almost normal. reasons: Scope 4: of the 220 terms, the whole-sound character words (clean, natural, vintage, clinical, sterile, lifeless, lush, musical, euphonic, transparency, hi-fi, lo-fi, organic texture, modern and others, about 11%) get a single listing clause. fixes: FLOW/CLARITY: "Others describe the whole sound, such as clean, natural or vintage. Some describe the balance from low to high, or how sharply a drum hit starts." -> delete it from paragraph 2. Clean, natural or vintage say something about the character of the sound, not one region. Words such as tight or snappy describe how fast a note starts and stops." This also improves scope. LANGUAGE: "where many instruments have the body of their sound" -> "where many instruments have the lower part of their notes, which makes them sound full". FLOW: "A tone word does not say what caused the sound." -> "Whatever the word, it describes what we hear, not what caused it."

comment: A strong, accurate lesson that covers the whole topic: reflections, decay, clarity, modes and the Schroeder frequency, absorption, diffusion, and isolation and noise. Every named term agrees with the glossary, and the opening is an everyday scene that ends on the topic's question. fixes: Accuracy: "each connect to their own volume control, called a channel, on a mixing board" -> "each connect to their own channel on a mixing board, with a fader that sets its volume". comment: An accurate, well-scoped lesson that follows the sound from studio to transmitter: links, modulation limit, processing, FM stereo and data, digital and television, then loudness rules. fixes: Accuracy: "A quiet tone, also too high to hear, tells a stereo radio to separate the two." -> "A quiet tone, too high for most people to hear, is the signal a stereo radio uses to separate the two." reasons: accuracy: 'Heavy, sealed walls keep outside noise out' and 'each voice is recorded on its own track' read as true of every show; they are common practice and should say 'usually' or 'often'; flow: paragraph 4 ('Not every episode is a free conversation...') moves to audiobooks, advertisements and animated films, which are not podcast episodes, so it leaves the episode thread for a moment; opening_closing: the opening (a listener hearing a talk show on a phone) is the same kind of scene as sibling 4090 (a listener hearing a radio show in a car).

reasons: Accuracy 4: the test-tools paragraph says meter/oscilloscope tests 'often show' a muted channel or wrong socket, which those tools do not usually reveal (those are found by looking, before testing). The ground-loop sentence says the equipment is 'connected to ground in two places', which blurs the real cause: two separate ground paths between the same pieces of equipment. Scope 4: methods, tests, intermittents, hum, digital/RF and root cause are all covered, but power problems (brownout, voltage sag, dirty power, voltage surge) and the feedback-control group (feedback suppressor, notch it, chase feedback) are missing or get only one word ('howl'). The crew slang group (dead, fried, toast, magic smoke) is not mentioned, not even in the closing. Flow 4: paragraph 2 joins three ideas (naming the symptom, two safety rules, reproducing the fault) with a weak 'so'. Paragraph 4 places 'simple mistakes' after the test tools, though they are checked first. Paragraph 6 is a two-sentence list of symptoms that could be moved without loss. Clarity 4: paragraph 3 names three methods (half-split, known-good substitution, signal tracing) in one paragraph, which is dense for a beginner. A beginner also cannot follow why grounding 'in two places' makes current flow in the audio cable.
comment: A strong, calm, mostly linear lesson. It covers the method from symptom to root cause, puts the safety rules early and passes the script cleanly (470 words, 8 paragraphs, 6 named terms, all matching the glossary). The polish items: the test-tools paragraph's order and claim, one clearer ground-loop sentence, and a lighter load in paragraph 3. Scope should name power problems and feedback control, and the crew slang could be mentioned in the closing. The swapped-wire cancellation idea also appears in sibling 3530 in nearly the same words, so reword one of them. Weighted 4.4 (B).
fixes: ACCURACY/FLOW: 'Test tools help prove where the fault is. A meter shows whether a wire is unbroken. An oscilloscope draws the shape of a test tone after it passes through equipment. These tests often show a simple mistake, such as a cable in the wrong socket or a muted channel. If not, the cause is often a cable or plug, because these move and bend the most.' -> 'Often the cause is a simple mistake, such as a cable in the wrong socket or a muted channel, so a careful look comes first. If not, test tools help prove where the fault is. A meter shows whether a wire is unbroken. An oscilloscope draws the shape of a test tone after it passes through equipment. The cause is often a cable or plug, because these move and bend the most.' ACCURACY/CLARITY: 'A steady low hum often means two pieces of equipment are connected to ground in two places, so a small current flows through the audio cable.' -> 'A steady low hum often means two pieces of equipment are connected to ground by two different paths, so a small current flows through the audio cable between them.' SCOPE/FLOW: 'Wireless microphones can lose their signal from a weak battery or strong radio signals nearby.' -> 'Wireless microphones can lose their signal from a weak battery or strong radio signals nearby. Power problems, such as a mains voltage that drops for a moment, can also cause clicks, resets or noise.' SCOPE (feedback): 'A loud howl usually means a microphone receives the sound of its own speaker.' -> 'A loud howl usually means a microphone receives the sound of its own speaker, and turning down the one frequency that howls can often stop it.' SCOPE (closing): 'The flashcards explain each step, the test tools, and the names of common faults.' -> 'The flashcards explain each step, the test tools, and the names of common faults, including the short words crews use for them.' CLARITY (paragraph 3 load): 'Checking the signal at each point until it disappears is called signal tracing. Each time, you change only one thing.' -> move the signal-tracing sentence to the start of paragraph 4 as 'Test tools make this checking exact. Checking the signal at each point until it disappears is called signal tracing.' and keep 'Each time, you change only one thing.' at the end of paragraph 3. SIBLING OVERLAP: 'A thin, hollow sound can mean one cable has its two signal wires swapped, so its sound partly cancels another copy of the same sound.' -> 'A thin, hollow sound can mean a wiring fault has turned one signal the wrong way, so it partly cancels another copy of the same sound.'

reasons: Accuracy 4: 'The same kind of timing problem happens between microphones' links buffer and clock timing to the different arrival times at two microphones, but these are different problems, so the link can mislead. Scope 4: placement covers only left and right. The depth / front-to-back / perspective / room-to-direct group (about 5% to 10% of the list, and in the Welcome text) is missing, and the null test and transient terms are not mentioned. Flow 4: several transitions are forced rather than earned: 'The same kind of timing problem', 'When the microphones work together', and 'So the main part is often the loudest' (this does not follow from masking). Clarity 4: 'preamplifier and a converter' are named with no plain description, and paragraph 3 packs buffers, latency and clocking into one paragraph. Language 4: 'turns its signal upside down' is figurative for a literal reader, and 'sharp sounds' is a vague sound adjective.
comment: A well-organized lesson. Its opening question (equipment, settings, mix, or hearing?) runs through the whole lesson, and it covers gain staging, latency, phase/polarity, stereo placement, masking and listening bias. All 5 named terms agree with the glossary, and the script passes (475 words, 8 paragraphs). It needs a front-to-back depth sentence for scope, a truthful bridge between the latency and microphone-timing paragraphs, plain descriptions of the preamplifier and converter, and two literal wording fixes. Weighted 4.2 (B).
fixes: ACCURACY/FLOW: 'The same kind of timing problem happens between microphones.' -> 'A different timing problem happens between microphones.' FLOW: 'When the microphones work together, each sound needs a place between the two speakers.' -> 'Once the microphones agree in time, each sound needs a place between the two speakers.' SCOPE: 'Other parts often go to the sides.' -> 'Other parts often go to the sides. A sound can also seem near or far, depending on how much room sound is heard with it.' FLOW: 'A loud sound can hide a softer one in the same frequency range. That is called level masking. So the main part is often the loudest.' -> 'A loud sound can hide a softer one in the same frequency range. That is called level masking. So engineers decide which part matters most and often make it the loudest.' CLARITY: 'Sound passes from the microphone through a preamplifier and a converter, and each step has a maximum level.' -> 'Sound passes from the microphone through a preamplifier, which raises its level, and a converter, which turns it into numbers. Each step has a maximum level.' LANGUAGE: 'A cable with two wires swapped turns its signal upside down, and then low frequencies cancel against the other microphone.' -> 'A cable with two wires swapped makes its signal go down when it should go up, and then low frequencies cancel against the other microphone.' LANGUAGE: 'with room left below its maximum for sharp sounds such as drum hits.' -> 'with room left below its maximum for sudden loud sounds such as drum hits.'

reasons: Accuracy 4: in paragraph 3, 'In both cases, the speakers make each voice clear rather than loud' follows a sentence about recording and online streaming, where room speakers play no part, so the logic is wrong. comment: A solid lesson that covers the whole topic. The check script passes with no failures or warnings (479 words, 7 paragraphs, average sentence 13.7 words). fixes: 1) Accuracy/flow, paragraph 3. Quote: 'The sound is often recorded or sent to people watching online. In both cases, the speakers make each voice clear rather than loud.' comment: A strong, accurate walk from set to final mix. fixes: 1) Accuracy: 'Around this time, the sound team, the director and the composer watch the film together.' -> 'Around this time, the director watches the film with the sound team and, often in a separate meeting, with the composer.' 2) Accuracy and flow: 'Once the sounds match the picture, each part is prepared in a room built for that step, often in one building.' -> 'While this matching goes on, the dialogue, effects and music are each prepared in a room built for that work, often in one building.' comment: Accurate and well scoped. It covers small-signal parameters, models, near/far-field and directivity measurement, the spinorama, power handling and production testing. The named terms agree with the glossary. Only small flow and wording polish is needed. Weighted 4.6 (A).

reasons: Accuracy 4: the closing claim about collecting files is stated as an absolute. comment: An accurate, plainly worded tour of the program's two-view idea. Grade B (weighted 4.1). The first half is a strong chain: two views, then tempo and warp, then instruments and devices. The second half breaks into short feature paragraphs, and the extension and MIDI-tools groups are missing. Combining the last three short paragraphs into one linked paragraph would free space for a sentence on MIDI tools and extensions, and fix flow, scope and the paragraph count together.

comment: A very good lesson. Grade B (weighted 4.4). The opening scene leads naturally into the question of how one recording becomes an instrument, and each named term is described before it is named. The glossary agreement is exact. The remaining polish: soften one either/or claim, give the library and format group a real sentence (it is the third-largest group), and spread the dense drum paragraph. At 480 words it is at the cap, so cut words elsewhere when adding.

reasons: Accuracy 4: the crosstalk sentence also blames a forward/back lean (zenith error) for crosstalk. Flow 4: 'The results are written in a log.' is tacked onto the bias paragraph, and the record-head/sync sentence jumps back to heads after the reference-tape idea. It also uses the same 'The flashcards explain each part in detail:' line as sibling 4450, and both siblings open with records. House rules 4: 7 named terms, above the standard's 2–6, and the lesson sits exactly at the 480-word cap, so any fix must cut words. The check script passed with 0 fails and 0 warns.
